Recruiter snapshot

Why hire me?

Six things a hiring manager can check in under a minute — each one traceable to my resume, offer letter or recommendation letter.

01

I think in positioning, not channels

Where a brand sits in its category decides what every channel afterwards costs. That's where I start, and it's why my campaign numbers held.

02

I've owned the full marketing mix

Brand communication, 360° campaign planning, out-of-home media, event funnels, content and paid acquisition — including a three-stage campaign built stage by stage.

03

I've branded a person, not just a company

Owned the personal brand strategy for the Group's Founder & Director — narrative, content pillars, platform authority — alongside the institute's own positioning. Most marketers meet that brief a decade in.

04

Marketing plus finance

PGDM dual specialisation in Marketing and Finance. I read a marketing budget the way the business reads it — cost, payback, contribution.

05

I negotiate, and I ship

Media rates, sites, vendors, printers, agencies and installation deadlines handled directly. Marketing plans die in delivery; mine went live.

06

Growth without a bigger budget

Spend came down while lead cost improved. My best campaign delivered leads 33% cheaper than the account average — that gap is where growth comes from.

Featured work

Business problem → strategy → execution → outcome.

Thirteen pieces of work, opened up. Metrics appear only where they were measured; where they weren't, I say so rather than inventing one.

Business problem

SIRE was a young education brand launching under Shivalik — a name Ahmedabad already trusted, but for real estate. There was recognition to borrow and no category position of its own: no clear answer to what the institute stood for, or who it was for.

Strategy

Settle the position before buying attention, then make every channel carry the same argument. Brand first, mix second — so paid, organic, events and physical media reinforced one story instead of running three.

Execution

Contributed to brand positioning and marketing communication working directly with the Group's Founder & Managing Director and leadership, then translated it into a 360° plan across social, content, paid social, out-of-home and event promotion. Developed the marketing creative for four separate course products — each with its own audience and promise — inside one visual system, so the institute read as a single brand rather than four campaigns.

Outcome

No isolated brand-lift study was commissioned, so I won't attach a number to the positioning itself. What is on record: a formal recommendation crediting a meaningful contribution to SIRE's brand positioning and marketing communication strategy. The downstream results sit in the projects below.

DisciplinesBrand positioningBrand architectureMarketing communication360° planningCreative developmentSenior stakeholder alignment

What I took from it

A brand with a clear position makes every channel cheaper. The work that looks least measurable is usually what makes the measurable work possible — and it's the part that lets a brand scale without spend scaling with it.

Business problem

In real estate, trust moves through people before it moves through companies. The Group had a name Ahmedabad already knew; its Founder & Director did not have a public voice in proportion to it. That left the institute's authority resting on a logo rather than on the person a buyer would actually be trusting.

Strategy

Treat the executive as a brand with its own positioning. Define what he stands for inside the category, fix the content pillars that prove it, and build platform authority deliberately — instead of posting whenever there was something to announce.

Execution

Owned the personal brand strategy for the Founder & Director: brand narrative, positioning, content pillars and messaging across platforms. Then planned and produced the content itself, building visibility in real estate and in the women-entrepreneurship space.

Outcome

Personal branding compounds slowly and wasn't measured separately inside my window, so there's no figure to quote. What changed immediately is structural: the institute gained a human voice, and one position now ran consistently through the company brand, the founder's presence and the course campaigns.

DisciplinesExecutive personal brandingBrand narrativeContent pillarsPlatform strategyThought leadershipMessaging

What I took from it

A company can state a position. A person can prove one. Getting a founder to say the same thing consistently, in his own voice, buys more credible reach than most paid budgets do — and it is the cheapest brand asset a business owns.

Business problem

Roughly ₹8,00,000 a month was going into paid acquisition across four course products. Nobody was asking whether that budget was buying enquiries the institute could enrol, or simply buying reach — and with a ₹7L+ monthly commitment, the answer mattered to the P&L, not just to marketing.

Strategy

Make cost per lead the only measure that counts, then treat the budget as something to be reallocated weekly rather than spent evenly. Build campaign variants per product and per geography so there is always a cheaper option to shift money into.

Execution

Ran the full Meta account: campaign structure by course product, pincode-level geo variants against broad targeting, evening dayparting, lead forms plus pixel tracking, and creative iteration against CPL. Reported monthly to the marketing team and Group leadership.

Outcome

1,981Leads captured in one month at an average CPL of ₹358.71, on ₹7.11L of spend — against the roughly ₹8L the account had been running at.

Where the thinking shows

The spread was the opportunity. Across the month my best campaign delivered leads at ₹238.79 and my worst at ₹589.66 — a 2.5× gap on the same product and the same offer. Averages hide that; only campaign-level CPL exposes it, which is why the budget got rebalanced toward the pincode-targeted and evening variants instead of spread evenly.

The audience data changed the creative. Clicks skewed hard to 18–24 year olds and heavily male, so the top-of-funnel work leaned into career-entry language rather than investor language — and the land-owner product got separated out with its own creative instead of competing for the same feed.

DisciplinesMeta AdsBudget ownershipCPL optimisationGeo & pincode targetingLead forms & pixelAudience analysisPerformance reporting

What I took from it

Efficiency is a growth lever, not a cost-cutting exercise. Cutting the blended CPL means more pipeline for the same money — and a marketer who can find the 2.5× hiding inside an account average is worth more than one who can only ask for a bigger budget.

Business problem

A street kiosk has no brand, no footfall data and no second chance — people either walk toward it or straight past it. We had a product, a location and no media budget, so attention had to be earned rather than bought.

Strategy

Use the one free distribution channel properly. Build content for how the algorithm actually distributes — format, hook, posting rhythm — so reach came from the platform instead of from spend, then convert that reach into physical footfall with posters at the point of decision.

Execution

Co-founded the venture and owned content strategy and creative production end to end: algorithm-optimised Instagram content that reached organic trending, plus promotional posters produced in-house and tied to the kiosk's location and hours.

Outcome

₹35,000+In sales within the first ten days, generated from organic reach — content that travelled without a rupee of media spend, converted into paying footfall at the kiosk. March 2026.

DisciplinesVenture buildingContent strategyCreative productionOrganic distributionOffline conversionRetail marketing

What I took from it

This is the closest I've come to owning a P&L, and it changed how I read every campaign since. Attention is only worth what it converts to — and the distance between a trending post and a paying customer is a design problem, not a luck problem. It also means I've sold something myself, not only marketed someone else's product.

Business problem

Paid reach was working, but the moment campaigns paused the brand went quiet. A new institute needs an audience it doesn't have to buy back every month.

Strategy

Treat social as brand equity rather than a posting duty. Lead with the formats the audience already watches, hold the brand's voice steady across all of them, and build the rhythm around what performed.

Execution

Content strategy, creative development and marketing communication across the page — hooks, formats and brand-consistent design produced in house.

Outcome

+6,000Owned audience grown from ~30,000 to 37,100 across the internship. One asset crossed 213,000 views.

What I took from it

Distribution comes from format, not frequency. Thirteen reels in a month reached 71,213 people, and the three that travelled furthest all showed the institute from the inside — the mentor, the jury room, the site visit — rather than advertising the course. An owned audience is a balance-sheet asset disguised as a marketing task.

Business problem

Education in real estate is sold on trust, and trust doesn't survive a static post. The institute needed people on screen — but no single format does every job, because a prospective student, an industry partner and a Gujarati-speaking parent are not persuaded by the same thing.

Strategy

Build a small system rather than a pile of one-off videos. Authority content from leadership to establish credibility, a campus film to make the place feel real, a plain walkthrough to answer the questions that stall an enrolment, and a vernacular cut to reach the audience English content never gets to.

Execution

Planned and produced the video content across formats — concept, script direction, shoot coordination and on-screen treatment — with one brand position running through all of them, so the institute reads as a single voice instead of four unrelated videos.

Outcome

Per-video performance wasn't reported separately, so I've shown the work rather than attach a number to it. What the monthly report does show: 13 reels in June alone, 71,213 organic reel reach, and video creative sitting among the best-performing ads in the paid account.

DisciplinesVideo content strategyFormat planningScript directionShoot coordinationVernacular marketingOn-camera direction

What I took from it

One position, four executions. The moment each format invents its own tone, the brand stops compounding — a campus film and a founder's talking head have to sound like the same institute, or you aren't building a brand, you're just making videos. Working in Gujarati also taught me that reach isn't only a budget problem; sometimes it's a language one.

Business problem

An education decision in Ahmedabad is local and high-consideration. A brand establishing itself needs to be physically present in the parts of the city its buyers move through — something a feed cannot do.

Strategy

Treat offline as a planned layer of the brand's mix, not an add-on. Choose sites on audience fit and visibility rather than availability, and time them with what the digital campaigns were saying.

Execution

Mapped available sites, held the vendor and agency conversations, negotiated rates and durations directly, then coordinated creative, printing, timelines and installation through to going live. Also developed the outdoor creative concept: a paired 10 × 15 ft board set designed to be read in sequence as traffic passes.

Outcome

No performance figures were published for the out-of-home work, so I've described the scope and responsibility instead of attaching numbers I can't stand behind. Sites, rates and the negotiation detail are available in conversation.

DisciplinesMedia planningRate negotiationVendor managementOOH creative conceptPrint & productionCampaign timing

What I took from it

Offline media is a negotiation business with a deadline attached. It made me sharper on cost, more direct with vendors, and much better at judging whether a plan can actually be delivered before I promise it.

Business problem

Indian real estate skews overwhelmingly male — my own campaign data put 85% of engagement with men. Women in Real Estate (WIRE) exists to change who enters the industry, which means reaching an audience the category's usual marketing has never spoken to.

Strategy

Programme before promotion. Make the speaker line-up the reason to show up, then market to a community rather than a list — because the goal was people who come back, not a one-off registration spike.

Execution

Supported planning and promotion of speaker-led sessions built to help women start and grow businesses in real estate: coordinating speakers, driving promotion across social channels, and working on attendee turnout and ongoing community engagement.

Outcome

Turnout and community engagement were the objectives and no public figures were released, so I've described the contribution rather than attach a number to it. Event detail available in conversation.

DisciplinesEvent marketingSpeaker coordinationCommunity buildingSocial promotionAudience development

What I took from it

The audience your data doesn't show you is often the one worth building for. Under-served segments respond to programming and belonging, not to persuasion — and a community you build is an acquisition channel nobody can outbid you for.

Business problem

Domain experts want to run paid seminars and webinars in their field, but a webinar is a hard sell: the audience is cold, the value is invisible until they attend, and one generic poster is asked to do every job at once. Here, an ex-recruiter's live interview masterclass for 2025–26 graduates in Gujarat, priced at ₹19.

Strategy

Stop making one creative do three jobs. Split the message by how warm the viewer is: one asset to make a cold graduate feel the problem, one to prove the class actually solves it, one to close on price, date and platform. Same event, three arguments.

Execution

Planned the event and promotion strategy end to end, then wrote and designed all three stages of the funnel — positioning, copy, offer presentation and layout — so each asset could be deployed to a different audience temperature rather than to everyone at once.

Outcome

The campaign is live for the 20 September session, so registration and conversion figures aren't in yet. What's shown here is the strategy and the creative; performance data goes up once the event has run.

DisciplinesFunnel designEvent marketingOffer & pricing presentationCopywritingCreative designCampaign planning

What I took from it

Cold traffic doesn't want your event — it wants its own problem named back to it. Price is only an argument at the end: leading with ₹19 to a stranger sells nothing, because they haven't agreed there's a problem yet.

Business problem

Two SaaS platforms were dependent on channels that scale only as fast as spend does. Organic demand was underbuilt on both.

Strategy

Build the asset rather than rent the traffic. Fix on-page foundations, map keywords to commercial intent rather than raw volume, then earn authority through quality rather than link count.

Execution

Owned SEO end to end — on-page work, keyword strategy and an off-page programme — tracking ranking movement on priority terms throughout.

Outcome

4×Organic traffic supported from roughly 25,000 to 100,000 monthly visits, with improved keyword rankings.

DisciplinesOrganic strategyCommercial keyword mappingOn-pageOff-pageRank tracking

What I took from it

The cheapest growth is the kind you build once. It taught me to hold a channel through the quiet months and defend it with a payback timeline instead of a weekly number.

Business problem

A food-delivery brand meets most of its customers on the worst day — the order is late, cold or wrong. That conversation is brand communication whether anyone designs it or not, and most companies leave it to a script that apologises and stalls.

Strategy

Treat the bot as a brand asset with a persona and a spending limit, not a deflection tool. Decide up front what it sounds like, what it is allowed to give away, and the exact moment it should stop talking and hand the customer to a person.

Execution

Built the full conversation architecture: five branches, a validated order-ID flow, a service-failure classifier, a recovery menu and a fallback that narrows twice before escalating. Persona — warm, brisk, accountable; apologises once, then fixes. Escalates on three unrecognised inputs, a human request, a food-safety complaint, or any refund above ₹2,000. Recovery budget: ₹500 settled without approval.

Outcome

A clickable prototype covering all eight assignment requirements, with the same flow logic reproduced as a build sheet for deployment. This is coursework, not a live product — there is nothing deployed and so nothing to measure. Click through it below.

Interactive · click any branch
DisciplinesService designConversation designBrand voiceService recoveryEscalation policyPrototyping

What I took from it

Service recovery is marketing’s most under-used channel — a complaint handled well buys more loyalty than the original sale did. And the budget question, how much a bot may give away before a human steps in, is a brand decision wearing an operations costume. Set it too low and you protect ₹500 while losing a customer.

Business problem

Dockfest is the institute's annual film festival. Every entry gets the same brief and the same audience, so the only real variable is whether a story can hold attention for its full run without a budget or a name behind it.

Strategy

Treat it like a campaign rather than an art project: decide the single feeling the film has to leave behind, then cut everything that doesn't serve it.

Execution

Conceptualised, shot and edited the film end to end — storyboarding, direction and post-production, working to the festival deadline.

Outcome

3rd placePlaced third among institute-wide entries and won a ₹10,000 cash prize. December 2025.

DisciplinesStorytellingStoryboardingDirectionVideo editingPost-production

What I took from it

Film and marketing run on the same constraint: you get a few seconds to earn the next few. Cutting my own footage taught me more about hooks and pacing than any advertising course did — and it shows in the reels.

Business problem

Live events are where a brand's promise either holds up in person or doesn't. Each of these needed the experience delivered on the day, with no second attempt.

Strategy

Be useful fast in a room I'd just joined: understand the running order, find the gap nobody had covered, and take it before it became a problem on stage.

Execution

Krafton India — stage coordination, player flow and technical setup for a large BGMI esports event. Samsung Electronics — on-ground promotions, customer engagement, product coordination and booth operations across multiple campaign days. Hungrito Food Fest — stage coordination and live operations. Narayana Business School — a micro-event planned and delivered on a fixed budget with a multi-member team.

Outcome

4Live activations delivered under tight timelines, including one where I owned the budget and the team end to end.

DisciplinesEvent marketingLive operationsCustomer engagementBudgetingTeam coordination

What I took from it

Experience marketing is where you learn what a brand actually feels like to a customer. It also taught me to plan for the version of the day that goes wrong.

How I work a problem

“Can you make it more creative?” Absolutely. Define creative.

That question is the job, so here is my answer to it — seven questions I work through before spending anyone's budget — each with the moment it came from.

01

Start with the business objective

Volume, margin, or entering a category? Marketing that doesn't name the objective can't be judged.

At SIRE the goal was enrolments, not reach.

02

Read the category

Who else competes for this decision, on what claim, and what has nobody credibly taken?

Four course products were separated by audience and promise, so they stopped competing in the same feed.

03

Decide the position

What does this brand stand for — and, harder, who is it not for?

Contributed to how SIRE was positioned and communicated under the Shivalik name.

04

Understand the buyer

What triggers the decision, what delays it, and where does it physically happen?

An education decision is local and high-consideration — which is why offline mattered.

05

Build the mix

Which combination of brand and demand channels fits, at what weight, over what horizon?

Paid social plus kiosks and billboards, saying the same thing at the same time.

06

Make the message carry it

One argument across every touchpoint, in the format each one actually rewards.

One reel built for the feed beat a month of scheduled posts.

07

Measure, then reallocate

One number decides it, agreed before launch. Then move budget toward what earns it.

CPL agreed up front — which is what made taking ₹1L out of spend defensible.

The short version

A brand with a clear answer costs less to grow. Get the position right and the media plan gets easier, cheaper and more obvious.
